clue.text: Eve could be deadly

parts.note: evening is the shade of night, and the poisonous plant belladonna carries the epithet 'deadly'

explanation.surface: A warning that Eve, temptress of Eden, might be lethal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Eve' as evening, the shadow cast by night; 'deadly' then completes the name of the poisonous plant, deadly nightshade.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly nightshade is the common name of belladonna, a poisonous plant of the potato family.

clue.text: It's half-way out, of course

parts.note: on a golf course of eighteen holes, the outward half ends at this hole

explanation.surface: Something is plainly halfway gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally'; read it as on a golf course, where the 'out' nine holes end halfway round.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf the front nine are the 'out' holes, so the last of them marks the halfway point of eighteen.

clue.text: Mendicants find no acceptance

parts.note: beggars ply their trade, and something nobody takes up or wants is said to be left the same way

explanation.surface: Beggars are turned away wherever they ask.
explanation.walkthrough: Mendicants are beggars, who live by asking for alms; something unwanted, with no takers, is also said to be left this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Beggars live by asking for alms, and an offer nobody takes up is said to lack takers this way.

clue.text: Beautiful women, but odd

parts.note: the trio of goddesses of beauty in Greek myth number an odd figure

explanation.surface: Some lovely women who are also rather strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like strange; read it as the odd number of these mythical beauties.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Graces, Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia, are goddesses of charm and beauty, three in number.

clue.text: The lass is not dressed for Ascot

definitions.text: The lass is not dressed for Ascot

indicators.note: dressed means put in order, so not dressed tells us the letters of the two words are out of order

explanation.surface: A girl turns up at the races without the proper outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not dressed' rearranges THELASS. Royal Ascot is an English race meeting famous for its elaborate hats, so a girl without one is improperly dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot dress code demands hats, so a girl bareheaded there is not properly dressed.

clue.text: Algerian governor is about to kiss the composer

indicators.note: the governor's title is about, wrapping round, the word for kissing

parts.note: a dey was the governor of Algiers under Ottoman rule
buss is an old word meaning to kiss

explanation.surface: A North African ruler is about to kiss a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is about to kiss' reads as 'is going to kiss'; split it, and 'is about' is the container signal while 'to kiss' gives the old verb for kissing.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Debussy was the French composer of Clair de Lune and La Mer.

clue.text: Smart abbreviation of one whom some talk of

definitions.text: Smart abbreviation of one whom some talk of

parts.words: Smart abbreviation of one whom some talk of
parts.note: a cocky know-all is a 'smart' something, and the song The British Grenadiers opens 'Some talk of Alexander', whose short form this is

explanation.surface: A clever shortening of the name of somebody people discuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' completes the phrase for a know-all; The British Grenadiers is a British marching song beginning 'Some talk of Alexander', and the answer is the short form of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart alec is a know-all, and the name is a familiar shortening of Alexander.

clue.text: Stopped and played like Orpheus

explanation.surface: A musician halted, having played like the mythical singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lute is also a clay cement for sealing joints, so luted means sealed up; Orpheus played the lyre-like plucked instrument, the lute.

clue.text: Mechanical aid to digest ?

parts.note: digest suggests the stomach, but a digest is a summary, and a device that compresses things would help make one

explanation.surface: A gadget to help the stomach process food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digest' looks like a verb about food; read it as a noun, a condensed summary, which a machine that condenses could help produce.
explanation.definitionFit: A condenser is an apparatus that reduces vapour to liquid, and to condense a text is to make a digest of it.

clue.text: Shady strips series of orgies under the Doges ?

definitions.text: series of orgies under the Doges

explanation.surface: Seedy strip shows and debauchery in old Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Slatted window shades are named after Venice, and blinds is slang for drunken sprees, so Venetian ones fall under the Doges.

clue.text: No fortunate, but none loftier

parts.note: taken as written
blest, an old spelling of blessed, means fortunate

explanation.surface: Nobody is luckier, yet nobody is more elevated either.
explanation.definitionFit: The most noble is the most lofty in character, so nothing stands loftier.

clue.text: Heaviest hive in Notts?

parts.note: a hive full of bees weighing a ton would be the heaviest, and the name splits that way; the place is in Nottinghamshire

explanation.surface: A question about which beehive in Nottinghamshire weighs the most.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as a hive's insects plus a ton, the heaviest weight; Notts is the short name for Nottinghamshire, an English county, where this town lies near Nottingham.
explanation.definitionFit: Beeston is a town in Nottinghamshire, just south-west of the city of Nottingham.

clue.text: They keep a girl on her toes

definitions.text: They keep a girl on her toes

parts.words: They keep a girl on her toes
parts.note: the idiom for keeping someone alert is taken literally: tall-heeled shoes tip the wearer forward onto her toes

explanation.surface: Something that keeps a young woman alert and busy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoes with tall heels raise the wearer's heel so her weight rests on the balls of the feet.

clue.text: Had he a small part in " The Vortex" ?

definitions.text: Had he a small part in " The Vortex" ?

parts.words: Had he a small part in " The Vortex" ?
parts.note: a vortex is a whirlpool, and a small swirl of water sounds like a man's name, as if he had a bit part in Noel Coward's play The Vortex

explanation.surface: A theatrical question about whether some actor played a minor role in Noel Coward's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vortex is a 1924 play by Noel Coward; read 'vortex' as a whirlpool and its 'small part' as a little swirl of current, spelt here as a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddie is a man's first name that sounds like eddy, a small whirl of water within a current.

clue.text: Lewis chiefly, if he's embracing her

definitions.text: Lewis chiefly, if he's embracing her

parts.words: Lewis chiefly, if he's embracing her
parts.note: put HE'S around the woman in question and you get the island group of which Lewis is the chief island

explanation.surface: A man named Lewis, mainly, is the one holding her close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lewis' seems a man's name, but it is the largest island of the Outer Hebrides, Scotland; HE'S wrapped round the answer makes HEBRIDES, and a man embracing his new wife fits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman on her wedding day is the one the groom embraces, the 'her' that HE'S surrounds to make the island chain.

clue.text: John, you seem hardly awake to your earth-moving power

definitions.text: John, you seem hardly awake to your earth-moving power

parts.words: John, you seem hardly awake to your earth-moving power
parts.note: John Bull personifies England, and someone hardly awake is a dozer, so England's dozing figure names an earth-moving machine

explanation.surface: Someone tells a sleepy John he does not realise how mighty he is.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bull is the stock figure personifying England; add a 'dozer', one who is dozing, and the result is a heavy machine that moves earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulldozer is a tracked tractor with a wide front blade for shifting earth.

clue.text: Brighter aspects of Attic life

parts.note: Attic suggests ancient Athens, but read it as a loft, whose brightest feature is its roof windows

explanation.surface: The cheerier side of life in ancient Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attic' is capitalised to suggest Attica and Athens; read it as a room under the roof, lit by windows set into the roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Roof windows let daylight into lofts and garrets, the bright spots of life up there.

clue.text: That mythical beast agen amok in the garden

definitions.text: That mythical beast agen amok in the garden

parts.note: the Hydra was the many-headed serpent of Greek myth

indicators.note: running amok, the letters of the dialect word for again are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: That legendary monster is running wild in the garden again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agen' is a dialect spelling of 'again'; 'amok' scrambles its four letters behind the many-headed monster, and the whole clue pictures that shrub growing wild in a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: The hydrangea is a garden shrub with large rounded heads of flowers.

clue.text: Short, but wordy characters

parts.note: shorthand signs are brief, yet each one stands for a whole word, so these characters are 'wordy'

explanation.surface: People who are small in stature but talk too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people and 'wordy' like talkative; read them as written signs that each represent a word, used in shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A logogram is a written sign standing for a whole word, as in shorthand or Chinese script.

clue.text: British saint turning up in fine form in Europe

definitions.note: stands for a country located in Europe

parts.note: St Alban is honoured as the first British martyr

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means the letters for top-rate are read from the bottom

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, in fine form, its figure one read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A British saint makes an appearance on the continent looking well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' suggests arriving, but it reverses A1 (first-rate, with the 1 read as I) to IA beneath ALBAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Albania is a Balkan country on the Adriatic coast of south-eastern Europe.

clue.text: A hundred to one Rita's send-up is TW3-type

indicators.note: in a down light a send-up sends the word upward, so it is read backwards

parts.note: the name Rita with its possessive s
I is the Roman numeral one
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone's parody of Rita is the kind of thing a sixties satire show would air, at long odds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send-up' suggests parody, matching TW3, but it reverses RITAS to SATIR. TW3 was That Was The Week That Was, a 1960s BBC satirical TV show.
explanation.definitionFit: That Was The Week That Was was a mocking satirical programme, so TW3-type means given to ridicule.

clue.text: It's low, but it's heavenly !

explanation.surface: Something that is at once base and divine.
explanation.definitionFit: It means the lowest point of fortune, and in astronomy the celestial point directly below the observer, opposite the zenith.

clue.text: It's d—— wet!

parts.note: the dash stands for the Greek letter named for d, and the same name is given to a marshy river mouth

explanation.surface: A mild curse at the soggy weather, swear word censored.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash looks like a censored 'damned'; read 'd——' as the Greek name of the letter d, which also names the wet, fan-shaped mouth of a river like the Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: Delta is the Greek letter d, and a river delta is a wet alluvial plain at a river's mouth.

clue.text: What a game to name the last bidder !

definitions.text: What a game to name the last bidder !

parts.words: What a game to name the last bidder !
parts.note: at an auction, the lot goes 'to' whoever bid last, so naming the winner sounds like the name of a numbers game

explanation.surface: An auctioneer's mock exasperation at having to announce who won.
explanation.walkthrough: At an auction the item, the lot, is knocked down 'to' the final bidder; that phrase runs together into the name of a game of chance like bingo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance in which numbers drawn are matched against players' cards.

clue.text: The virago's weapon ?

parts.note: a domineering woman is called by the name of a broad war hatchet, so her weapon carries her own name

explanation.surface: What a fierce, shrewish woman would fight with.
explanation.definitionFit: A formidable, overbearing woman is called by the name of the old war hatchet.

clue.text: Invest in ten chosen duets

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Put money into a set of ten selected musical duets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invest' looks financial; it means to endow or clothe, and the letters lie across 'chosen duets'.
explanation.definitionFit: To endue is to endow or furnish someone with a quality, as one invests them with it.

clue.text: Last letter I take to the Navy has strings attached

definitions.note: a phrase for a stringed instrument, standing for its noun

parts.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet
taken as written
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Someone joining the Navy finds the deal comes with conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has strings attached' sounds like a deal with conditions; it describes a stringed instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A zithern, the older form of zither, is a flat instrument with many strings stretched over a soundbox.

clue.text: Need Reg so roughly have gone back on his word ?

definitions.text: have gone back on his word

indicators.note: roughly says the letters of the two words are only approximately in place and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Reg seems to have broken his promise out of need.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges NEEDREG.
explanation.definitionFit: To renege is to break a promise or go back on an undertaking.

clue.text: Castle with two wings

parts.note: the chess piece also called the castle shares its name with a black crow-like bird, which has two wings

explanation.surface: A stately castle built with a pair of wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suggests a building's side extensions; the chess castle shares its name with a bird of the crow family.
explanation.definitionFit: The rook is the chess piece also called the castle, and a rook is a gregarious black crow.

clue.text: A dry procedure, the party's organizational scramble

definitions.text: A dry procedure, the party's organizational scramble

parts.words: A dry procedure, the party's organizational scramble
parts.note: in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the creatures run a chaotic race to get dry; a caucus is a party's organising meeting and the race is the scramble

explanation.surface: A dull political process, the party machine jostling for position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like dull; in Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland the Dodo organises a race in which everyone runs about to dry off after a swim.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caucus-race in Alice in Wonderland is run to get dry, and the term now means a confused contest of party politicking.
